{{Short description|none}}
'''Modern social statistics of Native Americans''' serve as defining characteristics of Native American life, and can be compared to the average United States citizens’ social statistics. Areas from their demographics and economy to health standards, drug and alcohol use, and land use and ownership all lead to a better understanding of Native American life. Health standards for Native Americans have notable disparities from that of all United States racial and ethnic groups. They have higher rates of disease, higher death rates, and a lack of medical coverage.<ref name="American Indian/Alaska Native Profile"/>

These health issues are matched by illegal drug abuse; abuse levels are higher than any other demographic group in the United States. [[Methamphetamine]] abuse on reservations was a particular area of concern for tribal and federal governments in the 2000s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.usdoj.gov/ndic/pubs28/29239/key.htm#Top |title=Key Findings-Indian Country Drug Threat Assessment 2008 National Drug Intelligence Center June 2008 Web 14 Sep 2009 |publisher=Usdoj.gov |date=2012-06-15 |access-date=2013-02-17}} *SITE CLOSED*see justice.gov's archive</ref> 

==General demographics==
Native American population demographics are studied by the federal government in conjunction with the Native Alaskan population. According to 2008 US Census projections, those who are Native American and Alaska Natives alone number 3.08 million of the total US population of 304 million, or 1.01 percent of the nation's entire population. Those who are Native American alone or in combination with other races measure as 4.86 million individuals, or 1.60 percent of the nation's entire population.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://factfinder.census.gov/servlet/QTTable?_bm=y&-qr_name=PEP_2008_EST_DP1&-geo_id=01000US&-ds_name=PEP_2008_EST&-_lang=en&-format=&-CONTEXT=qt |title="United States - DP-1. General Demographic Characteristics." American FactFinder. Web. 10 Oct. 2009 |publisher=Factfinder.census.gov |access-date=2013-02-17 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200210211222/http://factfinder.census.gov/servlet/QTTable?_bm=y&-qr_name=PEP_2008_EST_DP1&-geo_id=01000US&-ds_name=PEP_2008_EST&-_lang=en&-format=&-CONTEXT=qt |archive-date=2020-02-10 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The Native population continues to grow yearly. The Census Bureau projects that American Indian and Alaska Natives will reach 5 million individuals by 2065.<ref>{{cite web |first=Sarah |last=Berry |url=https://www.cdc.gov/omhd/populations/aian/aian.htm |title=OMHD Populations AIAN Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Web 15 Oct 2009 |publisher=Cdc.gov |access-date=2013-02-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129074901/http://www.cdc.gov/omhd/populations/aian/aian.htm |archive-date=2016-01-29 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

At the present time there are 574 [[federally recognized tribes]]. The population of Native Americans however extends beyond those with this federal recognition.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{Cite web|url=http://www.doi.gov/bia/ia_faqs.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091012132636/http://www.doi.gov/bia/ia_faqs.html|url-status=dead|title=Indian Affairs - FAQs U.S. Department of the Interior Home Page Web 18 Oct 2009|archive-date=October 12, 2009}}</ref> Certain tribes have much larger population bases than others. The United States Census has documented 1.93 million individuals that are American Indian or Alaskan Native alone (not in combination with other races) with specified tribes. The tribe with the largest population base, for 2008, was the tribe of [[Navajo people]] with 307,555 individuals. The [[Cherokee]] tribe had the second largest population, with 262,224 individuals. Follow in third and fourth are the [[Sioux]] tribe and [[Chippewa]] tribe with 114,047 individuals and 107,322 individuals, respectively. By 2020, [[Aztecs]] were the largest ethnic group in the Native American category, numbering 378,122 individuals.<ref>{{Cite web |publisher=United States Census Bureau |title=Census Bureau Releases 2020 Census Data for Nearly 1,500 Detailed Race and Ethnicity Groups, Tribes and Villages |url=https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2023/2020-census-detailed-dhc-file-a.html |access-date=2024-03-29 |website=Census.gov}}</ref> The remainder of the Native American tribes have populations below one hundred thousand. This does not account for those who do not have specified tribes or are of multiple races.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov |title=U.S. Census website |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]] |access-date=2013-02-17 }}</ref>

The distribution of age of Native Americans and Alaskan Natives differs from the general population of the United States, according to 2008 Census data. Of those who are strictly Native American or Alaskan Native, 28.3% are below the age of 18. 64.3% are between 18 and 64 years of age, while the remaining 7.4% are 65 years of age and older.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov |title=U.S. Census website |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]] |access-date=2013-02-17 }}</ref> This is a notably younger population than the overall population. The median age of Native Americans and Alaskan Native is 31.2, while the male median age is 30.0 and female median age is 32.8.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov |title=U.S. Census website |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]] |access-date=2013-02-17 }}</ref>

Native Americans and Alaskan Natives also differ in their [[household]] composition. Of the 795,764 documented households 68.5% are family households with the remaining 31.5% non family households. The 545,403 family households are divided between married-couple families, male-headed households, and female-headed households. Over half, 58.9% specifically, are married-couple families. Male-headed households are 10.8% of family households, while female-headed households are 30.3% of family households. Alternatively, non family households are constituted of those living alone and householders living with non family. Of the 250,361 non family households, 80.0% are living alone and 20.0% are non family not living alone.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov |title=U.S. Census website |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]] |access-date=2013-02-17 }}</ref>

==Economy and social status==
{{also|Native Americans and reservation inequality|Reservation poverty}}
The United States is home to 3.1 million Native Americans. In comparison to the rest of the population, this number is a very small amount (only .9%).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.adherents.com/adh_dem.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010205001400/http://www.adherents.com/adh_dem.html |url-status=usurped |archive-date=February 5, 2001 |title=Composite U.S. Demographics. Adherents.com 13 Mar 2001 Web 15 Sept 2009 |publisher=Adherents.com |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref> American Indians have historically lived in extreme poverty. With the rise of Indian gaming enterprises, the problem of poverty may have been variously addressed in select areas. Yet, while Native Americans have begun to take more control of their tribal economies, poverty on Indian Reservations is still a major issue. The U.S. Census in both 1990 and 2000 indicates that poverty has prevailed on reservations; to this day, Native Americans have the highest poverty and unemployment rates in the United States. The poverty rate of Native Americans is 25%.<ref name=autogenerated2>{{Cite web|url=https://www.census.gov|title=U.S. Census website|publisher=United States Census Bureau|website=[[United States Census Bureau]]}}</ref>

Incomes of Native Americans tend to be low, and unemployment rates are usually high. For example, the unemployment rate on the Blackfoot Reservation in Montana has been 69%. This is in comparison to the American national unemployment rate of 6.7% {{as of|2014|4|4|lc=y}},<ref name="BLS Economic News Release, April 4, 2014">{{cite web | title=Economic News Release | publisher=U.S. Department of Labor | url=http://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm }}</ref> or even during the worst part of the Great Depression at 25%.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.spotlightonpoverty.org/ExclusiveCommentary.aspx?id=0fe5c04e-fdbf-4718-980c-0373ba823da7 |title=Rodgers, Tom Native American Poverty: A Challenge Too Often Ignored Spotlight on Poverty 2009 Web 15 Sept 2009 |publisher=Spotlightonpoverty.org |access-date=2013-02-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130404211156/http://www.spotlightonpoverty.org/ExclusiveCommentary.aspx?id=0fe5c04e-fdbf-4718-980c-0373ba823da7 |archive-date=2013-04-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref> According to the 2000 Census, Indians living in Indian country have incomes that are less than half of the general U.S. population.<ref>Duthu, N. Bruce. American Indians and the Law. New York: Penguin Group, 2008. Print.  Page 118.</ref> The U.S. Census reports that the median income of households based on a three-year average from 2003-2005 was $33,627.<ref name=autogenerated2 /> 

In 1989, the median income of Native American households was $19,900. Average income varies by tribe and can range from $29,211 in the Osage tribe, to a mere $11,402 in the Tohono O’odham tribe.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m4021/is_n8_v18/ai_18538303/print |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080214134848/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m4021/is_n8_v18/ai_18538303/print |url-status=usurped |archive-date=February 14, 2008 |work=American Demographics |title=Russell, Cheryll Demo Snapshots: Native Americans Findarticles.com Media Central Inc. 1996 Web 15 Sept 2009 |issue=8 |volume=18 |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref> Over 20% of Native American reservation households make less than $5,000 annually while only 6% of the overall US population has an annual income of less than $5,000.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |url=http://www.perc.org/articles/article170.php |title=Anderson, Terry L. How the Government Keeps Indians in Poverty Perc.org. Wall Street Journal, 2009 Web 15 Sept 2009 |publisher=Perc.org |date=1995-11-22 |access-date=2013-02-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020173028/http://www.perc.org/articles/article170.php |archive-date=2012-10-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The average Native American family (3.41) is larger than the American national average,<ref name=autogenerated2 /> yet only 30% have health insurance.<ref name=autogenerated2 /> The quality of life for many Native Americans are often comparable to that of [[developing nations]].<ref name="auto"/> 

However, Indian tribes are becoming more economically independent in recent years. The [[impact of Native American gaming]] has been monumental, but non-gaming tribes have growing economies as well. For example, the [[Mississippi Choctaw]] Indians have incorporated industry into their economy. Automobile subassembly and plastic manufacturing are only two of the sectors in which the tribe is involved. Factories seem to contradict Indian culture, but ironically, industry helps culture thrive. By embracing industry, the Choctaw have been able to build a stable enough economy to prevent people from leaving the reservation and encourage people to come back, according to Chief Phillip Martin. Life on the tribe is more appealing because it is more secure. Jobs are readily available, and the tribe has revitalized public health, housing, and education.<ref name="Harvard 2008">Harvard. The State of the Native Nations. New York: Oxford UP, 2008. Print.</ref> Past federal policies have continually been detrimental to tribal economies,<ref>Duthu, N. Bruce. American Indians and the Law. New York: Penguin Group, 2008. Print.</ref> but [[self-determination]] has provided tribes with the independence and sovereignty to combat a history of poverty.<ref name="Harvard 2008"/>

According to the US Census, real per capita income has grown substantially in past decades. In 1970, the average real per capita income among Reservation Indians was $4,347. This figure grew to $6,510 in 1980, dipped to $5,959 in 1990, and grew again to $7,942 in 2000. However, the overall statistic for the United States has also steadily grown over this span of time. The total US real per capita was $13,188 in 1970 and $21,587. While economy on Reservations has improved, it is still significantly lower than that of the United States.<ref name="Harvard 2008"/>

The tribe with the lowest per capita income on a non-gaming Reservation is the [[Crow Creek Reservation]] in South Dakota with $4,043, but it also has a very low population of 1,846. The tribe with the highest per capita income on a non-gaming Reservation is the [[St. Regis Mohawk Reservation]] in New York. With a population of 2,581 {{as of|2008|lc=y}}, it averages $12,016 per year.<ref name="Harvard 2008"/> The least successful gaming Reservation has a lower per capita income than the Crow Creek Reservation: The Texas Kickapoo Reservation, population of 423, has an average of $3,398. The most successful gaming tribe is the [[Viejas Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians|Viejas]] Reservation in California; its population is 232 and averages $28,128 per capita income.<ref name="Harvard 2008"/> Therefore, population is insignificant when determining economic success. A better measure is geographic location.

{{further|Impact of Native American gaming}}

Further breakdown of poverty rates show that Native Americans are consistently the highest among each race. Reservation Indians have a 39% poverty rate; Non-Reservations, 26%; [[Black people|Black]], 25%, Hispanic/Latino of all races, 23%, [[Pacific Islander]], 18%, [[Asian people|Asian]], 13%; and [[White people|White]], 9%.<ref name="Harvard 2008"/>

==Location and lands==
[[File:US AIAN 2008 map.gif|thumb|350px|This map shows the population concentration of Native Americans and Alaskan Natives in 2008 by state, with darker shades of green indicating greater concentration.]]
The Native American population is not evenly spread across the nation. The greatest proportion live in the western regions of the United States, specifically 43%. The remainder live in the south, 31%, the midwest, 17%, and the northeast, 9%. This statistic demonstrates how the Native American population is concentrated into few general areas. This is further proven by the fact that over half of Native Americans live within ten states.<ref name= PDF>{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/prod/2002pubs/c2kbr01-15.pdf |title=The American Indian and Alaska Native Population: 2000 (2002): 4-12. The American Indian and Alaska Native Population 2000 US Census Bureau Web 15 Oct 2009 |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref> In 2000, the states with the largest Native American populations were California, Oklahoma, Arizona, Texas and New Mexico. Twenty-one states have Native American populations which constitute less than 1% over their overall population, including states such as Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and West Virginia.<ref name= PDF/>

Native Americans live in every different location, from reservations and rural areas to major urban centers. Reservations administered by the United States constitute about {{convert|56200000|acre|km2}} of land. This is broken into about 326 areas, ranging greatly in size from millions of acres to slightly over {{convert|1|acre|m2|adj=on}}. In addition to these federal reservations, there are allotted lands, lands under restricted status, and state Indian reservations.<ref name=autogenerated1 />

The land-owning segment of the Native American population continues to increase, which in the later 1900s nearly doubled each decade.<ref>Olson, James Stuart. Native Americans in the twentieth century. Provo, Utah: Brigham Young UP, 1984. Print.</ref> Private property owners include those who live in cities or urban centers. The two specific places with the largest Native American populations are the Los Angeles-Long Beach area, followed by New York City; each are home to over 50,000 Native Americans.<ref name= PDF/> Other large concentrations of urban Native Americans include Phoenix, Arizona and Anchorage, Alaska.<ref>Waldman, Carl. Atlas of the North American Indian. 3rd ed. New York: Checkmark Books, 2009. Print.</ref>

==Health standards==
{{main|Native American health}}
{{further|New World syndrome}}

Native Americans require medical care and have health concerns similar to many other United States demographics. From all ages of American Indians or Alaska Natives, approximately 12% were found to be in fair or poor health in 2005.<ref name= CDC>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/fastats/indfacts.htm |title=FASTSTATS - Health of American Indian or Alaska Native Population. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Web 15 Oct 2009 |publisher=Cdc.gov |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref> There are known [[health disparities]] between the Native American population and the rest of the United States. Reasons for these health disparities include "cultural barriers, geographic isolation, inadequate sewage disposal, and economic factors."<ref>The Health Care Challenge: Acknowledging Disparity, Confronting Discrimination, and Ensuring Equality. United States Commission on Civil Rights, Sept. 1999.</ref> However, there are many indicators that the health status of Native Americans has greatly improved in the previous decades.

Native American tribes have received much needed attention from the medical field due to the increasing [[infant mortality rate]] among their people, while the American nation sees this demographic overall on the decline.<ref name="Seattle News">{{cite web|author=Vanessa H |url=http://www.seattlepi.com/local/403196_tribes12.html |title=Native American death rates soar as most people are living longer. Seattle news, sports, entertainment seattlepi.com - Seattle Post-Intelligencer Web 14 Sept 2009 |publisher=Seattlepi.com |date=2009-03-11 |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref> The infant mortality rate of American Indians and Native Alaskans is 8.6 for every 1,000 live births. This is greater than the average infant mortality rate of all ages of 6.9, all measured in 2005.<ref name= infant>{{cite web | title=Infant Mortality and American Indians/Alaska Natives | publisher=The Office of Minority Health | url=http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/templates/content.aspx?ID=3038 | date=July 29, 2013 | access-date=March 31, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130814234741/http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/templates/content.aspx?ID=3038 | archive-date=August 14, 2013 | url-status=dead }}</ref> Native American infants suffer from [[Sudden Infant Death Syndrome]] at double the rate of their white counterparts. For congenital malformations and low birth weight, Native Americans infants suffer at a ratio of 1.3 to non-Hispanic whites.<ref name= infant/> Low birth weight was observed in 7.3% of births in 2005.<ref name=CDC/> Also notable is the fact that as the age of the birth mother increases, the ratio of Native American infant mortality to non-Hispanic white infant mortality increases.<ref name= infant/>

In 2005, Native Americans recorded 14,037 deaths. This translates to 438.5 deaths per 100,000 individuals.<ref name=CDC/> Within the United States region, Native American men have been found to be dying at the fastest rate of all people. The [[life expectancy]] of a Native American man is 71 years, six below the expectancy of a white male in the United States. Women fare at a similar level, with their death rate growing 20% over fifteen years of American national decline.<ref name="Seattle News"/> The leading causes of death among Native Americans (American Indians and Alaskan Natives) are heart disease, cancer and unintentional injury. The rate of suicide is also a significant concern, as it is above the American national average.<ref name= CDC/>

Native Americans also face a disproportional share of certain diseases. [[Native American disease and epidemics]] are commonly thought of as being alcoholism on tribal lands and surrounding areas. Many other diseases, such as diabetes, have a prominent presence among Native Americans.<ref name="American Indian/Alaska Native Profile"/> Native American children, in 2006, received "the recommended doses of vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella, Hib, polio, and chicken pox at the same rate as non-Hispanic White children."<ref name="Immunizations and American Indians/Alaska Natives">{{cite web | url=http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/templates/content.aspx?ID=3029 | title=Immunizations and American Indians/Alaska Natives | publisher=The Office of Minority Health | date=October 4, 2012 | access-date=March 31, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140331101355/http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/templates/content.aspx?ID=3029 | archive-date=March 31, 2014 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

Out of the single race population of Native Americans and Native Alaskans, about 16.8% of individuals have a [[disability]]. The majority of those with disabilities are in the 18- to 64-year-old age range, though this is also the largest demographic. For those age 18 and under, about 6% have a disability. About 17.9% of those American Indian and Alaska Natives ages 18 to 64 have a disability. Disabilities are far more prevalent in the eldest age range, 65 years and older, but this is a normal trend due to the effect of diseases on aging demographics.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov |title=U.S. Census website |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]] |access-date=2013-02-17 }}</ref> Native Americans also have high rates of mental health challenges. For instance, "Native Americans report themselves as under "frequent mental stress" 20 percent more than other populations."<ref>Project, Harvard, Eric C. Henson, Jonathan B. Taylor, Catherine E. A. Curtis, Stephen Cornell, Kenneth W. Grant, Miriam R. Jorgensen, Joseph P. Kalt, and Andrew J. Lee. The State of the Native Nations Conditions under U.S. Policies of Self-Determination. New York: Oxford UP, USA, 2007. Print.</ref>

There are many other health behaviors that are present in different rates in the Native American demographic. Out of all races and ethnic groups, Native Americans have the highest rate of [[smoking]]. As of 2008, about 32.2% of Native American adults smoked. This is in contrast to a rate of 21.8% for white adults. The high prevalence of smoking is also present in the Native American youth, as 23.1% of the youth smoke. Additionally, Native Americans had the highest rate of [[smoking and pregnancy|smoking during pregnancy]], at 17.8%. Smoking itself plays into Native American culture, therefore it is a challenging health concern.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lungusa.org/site/pp.asp?c=dvLUK9O0E&b=35999|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090601041530/http://www.lungusa.org/site/pp.asp?c=dvLUK9O0E&b=35999|url-status=dead|title=Smoking and American Indians/Alaska Natives Fact Sheet - American Lung Association site. Home - American Lung Association site Web 18 Oct 2009|archive-date=June 1, 2009}}</ref> Other health behaviors that contribute to the current health status include the high rates of obesity and generally low rates of physical activity.<ref>United States. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Vital and Health Statistics. Health Characteristics of the American Indian and Alaska Native Adult Population. By Patricia M. Barnes. 356th ed. 2005. Print.</ref>

Studies frequently note “a frequency of poor health and limited health care options” for Native Americans in the United States.<ref name="American Indian/Alaska Native Profile">{{ cite web | url=http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/templates/browse.aspx?lvl=2&lvlID=52 | title=American Indian/Alaska Native Profile | publisher=The Office of Minority Health | date=September 17, 2012 | access-date=March 31, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120913075542/http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/templates/browse.aspx?lvl=2&lvlID=52 | archive-date=2012-09-13 | url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Insurance]] coverage is held by the majority of Native Americans, but 33% of American Indians and Alaska Natives do not possess health insurance. About 36% did have private health insurance to cover their medical care, while 24% relied on Medicaid provided through the federal government.<ref name="American Indian/Alaska Native Profile"/> In addition to these services available to all Americans, the need for health care for Native Americans has been addressed by the American government. Currently there is a division of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services called the [[Indian Health Service]]. The IHS serves to provide health care services and administer various medical programs. Although this service serves many Native Americans, health care is still lacking for the masses. 33% of Native Americans reportedly did not have health insurance in 2007.<ref name="American Indian/Alaska Native Profile"/>

===Substance abuse===
{{Further|Alcohol and Native Americans|Methamphetamine and Native Americans}}
In 2002, Native Americans and Alaskan Natives were at a much higher risk than other minority populations for heavy drinking, binge drinking, and alcohol dependence.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/DEPRStrategicPlan/BriefingBook2.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070829002020/http://pubs.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/DEPRStrategicPlan/BriefingBook2.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 29, 2007|title=National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism|date=July 14, 2006|website=pubs.niaaa.nih.gov}}</ref> A study carried out from 2002 to 2005 reported that 10.7 percent of all Native American and Alaskan Native age groups suffered from alcohol use disorder, whereas 7.6 percent of other ethnic groups reported the same disorder.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.oas.samhsa.gov/2k7/AmIndians/AmIndians.htm|title=Substance Use and Substance Use Disorders among American Indians and Alaska Natives, SAMHSA, Office of Applied Studies<!-- Bot generated title -->|access-date=2009-10-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091202075411/http://oas.samhsa.gov/2k7/AmIndians/AmIndians.htm|archive-date=2009-12-02|url-status=dead}}</ref> Alcoholism is a particular issue among Native American women. General statistics indicate that Native American women drink less than men; however, specific tribal social norms and location cause this to vary among individuals.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pubs.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/arh26-4/251-256.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060212013242/http://pubs.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/arh26-4/251-256.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 12, 2006 |title=Minority Women and Alcohol Use |publisher=Pubs.niaaa.nih.gov |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref>

As a result, [[fetal alcohol spectrum disorder]] rates are higher than the national average in some tribes.<ref name="download.ncadi.samhsa.gov">{{cite web |url=http://download.ncadi.samhsa.gov/Prevline/pdfs/SMA06-4245.pdf |title=Substance Abuse and Mental Health Publications&#124; SAMHSA Store |publisher=Download.ncadi.samhsa.gov |date=2011-11-19 |access-date=2013-02-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527134028/http://download.ncadi.samhsa.gov/Prevline/pdfs/SMA06-4245.pdf |archive-date=2010-05-27 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Among tribes in Alaska, the rate of fetal alcohol syndrome, 5.6 every 1,000 births, is nearly four times higher than non-Indians' rate, 1.5 every 1,000 births.<ref name="download.ncadi.samhsa.gov"/> Overall, 11.7% of Native American and Alaskan Native deaths are alcohol-related, which includes traffic accidents, alcoholic liver disease, homicide, suicide, and falls.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nbcnews.com/id/26439767 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130227000936/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/26439767 |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 27, 2013 |title=1 in 10 Native American deaths alcohol related |publisher=NBC News |date=2008-08-28 |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref>

==== Other drugs ====
Native Americans are more likely than other ethnic groups to report past year illicit drug abuse.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.usdoj.gov/ndic/pubs28/29239/key.htm#Top |title=USDOJ: National Drug Intelligence Center |publisher=Usdoj.gov |date=2012-06-15 |access-date=2013-02-17}} *SITE CLOSED*see justice.gov's archive  at http://www.justice.gov/archive/ndic/</ref> Mexican drug-trafficking organizations are the main suppliers of illegal substances to reservations in Indian Country and presumed growers of marijuana on reservations.<ref name="usdoj.gov">{{cite web|url=http://www.usdoj.gov/ndic/pubs28/29239/drugover.htm#DTOs |title=USDOJ: National Drug Intelligence Center |publisher=Usdoj.gov |date=2012-06-15 |access-date=2013-02-17}} *SITE CLOSED*see justice.gov's archive</ref> Drug-trafficking organizations run by African-American, Asian, and Native American gangs and criminal groups also smuggle and supply on-reservation drug retailers with inventories of marijuana, ice methamphetamine, cocaine, and heroin.<ref name="usdoj.gov"/>

The most commonly abused drug on reservations is [[marijuana]] because of its ready availability.<ref name=autogenerated3>{{cite web|url=http://www.usdoj.gov/ndic/pubs28/29239/distro.htm#Abuse |title=USDOJ: National Drug Intelligence Center |publisher=Usdoj.gov |date=2012-06-15 |access-date=2013-02-17}} *SITE CLOSED*see justice.gov's archive</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ajph.aphapublications.org/loi/ajph|title=American Journal of Public Health (AJPH) - List of Issues|website=American Public Health Association (APHA) publications}}</ref> The number of Native Americans seeking help for marijuana addiction increased from 1,119 to 2,147 from 2003 to 2007.<ref name=autogenerated3 /> It is a potentially alarming statistic in the face of declining rates of reported marijuana use among 12- to 17- and 18- to 25-year-olds nationwide.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.drugabuse.gov/InfoFacts/nationtrends.html |title=Nationwide Trends &#124; DrugFacts &#124; National Institute on Drug Abuse |publisher=Drugabuse.gov |access-date=2013-02-17}}</ref> Recently, methamphetamine cartels have targeted Native American communities due to conflicts in jurisdiction between tribal, state, and federal law enforcement agencies that complicates the prosecution of methamphetamine producers and distributors. The resulting spike in rates of methamphetamine abuse and addiction has made the drug a law enforcement priority on many reservations in the American West, particularly the [[Wind River Indian Reservation]] of [[Wyoming]], and the [[Crow Nation]], [[Blackfeet Indian Reservation|Blackfeet Nation]], and [[Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation]] of [[Montana]].
